a: the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule
t: Dating John: the fifteenth year of Tiberius
p: Tiberius became emperor in AD 14, so his fifteenth year falls about AD 28 or 29.
b: Tiberius succeeded Augustus in August of AD 14. Counted from then, his fifteenth year runs from late AD 28 to AD 29. Some scholars count from AD 11 or 12, when Tiberius began to share power in the provinces, which gives AD 26 or 27; others reckon by the Syrian or Jewish calendar year, which moves the date by a few months. Either way John began preaching about AD 27 to 29, and Jesus' public work followed soon after. Luke is the only Gospel writer to give a date that historians can check against the Roman calendar. He dates the moment the way Greek historians did, by naming the rulers in office (Thucydides opens the Peloponnesian War with a priestess, a magistrate and an archon), and also the way Israel's prophetic books did (Jeremiah 1:1–3; Hosea 1:1).

p: Pilate governed Judea for Rome from AD 26 to 36. A stone found at Caesarea in 1961 gives his title.
b: After Herod's son Archelaus was removed in AD 6, Judea, Samaria and Idumea were ruled by Roman governors. Pilate held the post from about AD 26 to 36. A building inscription found in the theater at Caesarea in 1961 names him "Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judea," so his formal title was prefect; Tacitus and later writers call such governors procurators, and Luke uses the general verb "to govern" (hēgemoneuō). Josephus and Philo describe him as harsh and stubborn toward Jewish customs. Luke names him here, at the start, because he will judge Jesus at the end (23:1–25).

t: Herod Antipas, ruler of a quarter
p: This Herod is Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39.
b: When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, Rome divided his kingdom among three sons. Archelaus received Judea (and lost it in AD 6), Antipas received Galilee and Perea, and Philip the lands northeast of the Lake of Galilee. A "tetrarch" was originally the ruler of a fourth part of a country; by Jesus' day it meant a minor prince under Rome, ranked below a king. Mark calls Antipas "king" in the popular way (Mark 6:14); Luke uses the correct title. Antipas is the Herod who imprisons John (3:19–20), wonders about Jesus (9:7–9), is called "that fox" (13:32) and questions Jesus at his trial (23:6–12). Philip built Caesarea Philippi and ruled peacefully until AD 34.

p: Critics said Luke confused him with a king killed in 36 BC. An inscription from Abila points the other way.
b: Josephus tells of a Lysanias, ruler of Chalcis, executed by Mark Antony in 36 BC, sixty years before John. Older critics therefore accused Luke of a blunder. But Josephus also speaks of "Abila of Lysanias" as a territory still known by that name under the emperors Claudius and later (Antiquities 19.275; 20.138), and a Greek inscription from Abila, west of Damascus, dated in the reign of Tiberius, mentions "Lysanias the tetrarch." Most scholars now accept that a second, later Lysanias ruled Abilene in Tiberius' time, as Luke says, though little else is known of him.

a: Annas and Caiaphas held the high priesthood
p: The Greek says "in the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas," one office with two names.
b: Annas (Hebrew Hanan) was high priest from AD 6 to 15, when the Roman governor removed him. Caiaphas, his son-in-law (John 18:13), held the office from about AD 18 to 36, the longest term of the century, which suggests close cooperation with Pilate. Five of Annas' sons also became high priest (Josephus, Antiquities 20.198), and he stayed the head of the family that ran the temple. Luke names both because Annas still held the real power; in Acts 4:6 he even calls Annas "the high priest." In 1990 a family tomb in Jerusalem yielded an ossuary (bone box) inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas"; many think it is this Caiaphas, though the reading of the name is debated.
orig: ἐπὶ ἀρχιερέως Ἅννα καὶ Καϊάφα (epi archiereōs Hanna kai Kaiapha)

a: a word from God came to Zechariah's son John
p: Luke introduces John with the formula of the prophetic books: the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, Hosea, Jonah.
b: The Greek Old Testament opens many prophetic books with "the word of God (or of the LORD) that came to" a prophet, often after a list of reigning kings (Jeremiah 1:1–3; Hosea 1:1; Micah 1:1). Luke's long list of rulers followed by "a word from God came to John" presents John as the last of Israel's prophets, called in the same way. Only Luke tells of John's birth to the priest Zechariah (1:5–25, 57–80) and says he lived in the wilderness until he appeared to Israel (1:80). Jesus later calls him a prophet and "more than a prophet" (7:26).
orig: ἐγένετο ῥῆμα θεοῦ ἐπὶ Ἰωάννην (egeneto rhēma theou epi Iōannēn)

t: John's baptism, in Luke and in Josephus
p: Josephus also describes John's baptism, but says it was a washing of the body for those already made right by justice.
b: The Jewish historian Josephus, writing about AD 94, praises John as "a good man" who urged Jews to practice virtue, justice toward one another and reverence toward God, and "so to come to baptism." He adds that the washing was not to win pardon for sins but to purify the body, once the soul had already been cleansed by right living (Antiquities 18.116–119). Luke, like Mark, ties the baptism to repentance and forgiveness. The two accounts may describe the same practice from different angles: the outward washing marked an inward turning. Jewish purity washings were repeated; John's baptism, so far as we know, was given once and by another person, which was new. On Christian baptism and John's, see the cards at Matthew 3 and Acts 19.

p: The noun for "forgiveness" is aphesis, "release." Luke uses the same word twice in Jesus' first sermon (4:18).
b: Aphesis means a letting go: the release of a prisoner, the cancelling of a debt, the freeing of slaves in the year of jubilee (Leviticus 25:10 in the Greek Old Testament) and the forgiving of sins. English needs two words, "forgiveness" and "release," so the link is easy to miss. Luke uses it for sins here and in 1:77 and 24:47, and in 4:18 for "release to the captives" and the crushed sent away "free" (literally "in release"). For Luke, forgiveness is a kind of liberation.

a: A voice is shouting in the wilderness
t: Isaiah 40, and why Luke quotes more of it
p: Matthew and Mark quote one line. Luke goes on through Isaiah 40:5, to all flesh seeing God's salvation.
b: The quotation follows the Greek Old Testament, which joins "in the wilderness" to the voice; the Hebrew joins it to the command, "In the wilderness clear the way of the LORD!" (Isaiah 40:3). The Qumran community read the Hebrew that way and went out to the desert to prepare the way by studying the Law (Community Rule, 1QS 8.13–16). Luke alone carries the quotation on through 40:4–5, to end on the whole human race seeing God's salvation. The Hebrew of 40:5 says the LORD's glory will be revealed "and all flesh will see it, all together" (Isaiah 40:5); the Greek says "the salvation of God." Luke has already had Simeon see that salvation (2:30) and will end Acts with it: "this salvation from God has been sent out to the Gentiles" (Acts 28:28).

p: In Isaiah the road is for the LORD, YHWH. In Luke's Greek it is for "the Lord," and the next scenes point to Jesus.
b: The Greek Old Testament has no divine name; it writes kyrios, "Lord," where the Hebrew has YHWH. This site renders kyrios in New Testament quotations as "the Lord" and gives the Old Testament wording in a note. In Isaiah, God himself comes back to his people through the desert. Luke has already called Jesus "Christ the Lord" (2:11) and John the one who would go "before the Lord" (1:76), so his readers hear the road being prepared for Jesus, without Luke saying it outright.

t: Mountains brought low, the lowly lifted up
p: The verb is the one Mary used for the mighty brought down. Luke's reversals start in Isaiah's road-building.
b: Tapeinoō, "make low, humble," is the verb of Mary's song, where God brings down rulers and lifts up "the lowly" (tapeinous, 1:52). Jesus repeats the reversal as a rule: "Everyone who raises himself up will be brought low" (14:11; 18:14). Isaiah's image is of engineers leveling a royal highway. Luke's readers would hear more: the coming of God flattens human pride and raises the bowed down.

p: In Matthew John aims "offspring of vipers" at Pharisees and Sadducees. In Luke he says it to all the crowds.
b: Matthew 3:7 and Luke share almost word for word the speech that follows, so most scholars think both drew it from a common source (often called Q; see the topic page on the Synoptic problem). Matthew sets it against the religious leaders; Luke gives it to everyone who came out. Many scholars think Luke kept the original setting and Matthew sharpened it; others think the reverse. Luke's version makes the warning universal: no one is safe from the coming judgment just by turning up for the rite. Vipers fleeing a field fire is the picture behind "run from the coming anger."

p: John warns against trusting in descent. It is an argument inside Israel, made by an Israelite prophet.
b: Israel's prophets had long warned that belonging to the people did not guarantee God's favor (Amos 9:7; Jeremiah 7:4; Micah 3:11). Later rabbis taught the "merit of the fathers": God's love for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob covers their children. John does not deny that Abraham matters; he says God can make new children for Abraham whenever he wants. Many scholars note a wordplay that works in Hebrew and Aramaic: "sons" (banim, Aramaic bnayya) and "stones" (avanim, abnayya). Isaiah 51:1–2 already called Abraham the rock from which Israel was cut. Luke later shows Jesus calling a bent woman and a tax collector "a daughter of Abraham" and "a son of Abraham" (13:16; 19:9), restoring Jews on the edge to the family.

a: the ax already lies against the root of the trees
p: A woodsman has set his ax at the base of the trunk, ready to swing. Judgment is not far off; it has begun.
b: The words are the same as Matthew 3:10, apart from Luke's added "yes" (Greek kai, "even"). Trees as nations and fruit as conduct are old prophetic pictures (Isaiah 10:33–34; Jeremiah 11:16; Hosea 9:16). John's point is urgency. Jesus picks up the image in the parable of the fig tree that gets one more year (13:6–9), where judgment is delayed for the sake of mercy, but not cancelled.

a: Then what are we to do?
t: The question that runs through Luke-Acts
p: Three groups ask John the same question. Luke's second volume repeats it at Pentecost and in a Philippian jail.
b: Only Luke records 3:10–14. Crowds, tax collectors and soldiers each ask, "What are we to do?" Luke makes this the natural response to a call to repent, and he repeats it: a lawyer and a ruler ask Jesus what they must do to inherit eternal life (10:25; 18:18); the crowd at Pentecost asks Peter, "What are we to do, brothers?" (Acts 2:37); the jailer asks Paul and Silas what he must do to be saved (Acts 16:30); Paul asks the risen Lord what to do (Acts 22:10). The answers are concrete. John does not tell anyone to leave home or job, only to change how they treat others in the work they already do.

p: The tunic was the long shirt worn next to the skin. Someone with a spare one had more than the poorest.
b: Ordinary people wore a tunic (chitōn) and, over it, a cloak (himation) that also served as a blanket (Exodus 22:26–27). A second tunic was a modest extra, not wealth, which makes John's demand bite: generosity begins with ordinary surplus, not with riches. Food is treated the same way. Luke gives sharing with the poor great weight (12:33; 14:13; 18:22; 19:8) and shows it in the first church (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–35). When Jesus sends out the Twelve he tells them not to take two tunics (9:3).

p: In Galilee they collected tolls and duties for Herod Antipas; in Judea they worked inside Rome's system.
b: Rome and its client kings often sold the right to collect tolls and indirect taxes to contractors, who hired local agents. The agents paid the contract price and kept what they could collect above it. That system invited abuse and made the collectors hated as collaborators and cheats. Jewish sources class them with robbers: the Mishnah forbids taking change from a tax collector's money chest (Mishnah Bava Kamma 10:1). Luke shows tax collectors coming to John, and later many of them listen to Jesus (7:29; 15:1). Zacchaeus is a chief tax collector (19:2).

a: beyond the amount you have been assigned
t: Collect what you are owed, no more
p: John does not tell tax collectors to quit. He tells them to stop overcharging.
b: To diatetagmenon means "what has been laid down": the official rate in the contract. Overcharging was how agents got rich, so this was a real cost. The same moral line appears when Zacchaeus promises to pay back four times what he took by fraud (19:8). Whether John's answer means that collecting taxes for a foreign power was acceptable work is a question Luke does not raise; Jesus will say, "pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar" (20:25).
orig: τὸ διατεταγμένον (to diatetagmenon), 'what has been ordered'

p: Probably not Roman legionaries, since no legion was based in Judea before 66. More likely auxiliaries or Herod's troops.
b: Luke's Greek is a participle, "those serving in the army," not the usual noun for soldiers. In Galilee and Perea Herod Antipas kept his own troops, some of them Jewish; in Judea the Roman governor relied on auxiliary troops recruited mostly from the Gentile cities of Samaria and the coast. Some scholars think these men guarded tax collectors, which would explain why they come right after them. Either way they were Jews or Gentiles in the service of a power that taxed the poor. John again tells them how to do the job, not to leave it. The question whether a believer may serve as a soldier is set out on this chapter's card.

a: Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges
p: Two rackets: money by threats, and money by false accusations. Zacchaeus admits to the second.
b: Diaseiō means "shake violently," and in the papyri it is used for extorting money by intimidation. The KJV renders it "Do violence to no man," which Christian pacifists later read as a ban on violence in general; the context is about money. Sykophanteō is the source of English "sycophant": originally an informer who brought false charges to get a share of the fine or a bribe. Zacchaeus uses the same verb when he says, "if I have squeezed anything out of anyone by false charges" (19:8). The soldiers' wages (opsōnia, a soldier's ration money) were low, which tempted them to make it up by force.

a: could John himself be the Messiah?
p: Luke shows people wondering. John 1:20 has John deny it plainly, and some later groups did honor John above Jesus.
b: Luke says the whole people were "full of expectation." Jewish hopes in this period were varied: a king from David's line, a priestly anointed one, a prophet like Moses, or God himself coming (the Dead Sea Scrolls expect more than one figure). John's priestly birth and prophetic power made some ask. All four Gospels make John point away from himself, and the Fourth Gospel has him say, "I am not the Messiah" (John 1:20). The care with which the Gospels place John below Jesus suggests that some of John's followers held him in very high honor; Acts meets disciples who knew only John's baptism (Acts 18:25; 19:1–7). The Mandaeans, a small religious community of Iraq and Iran, still revere John as a prophet.

a: untie the strap of his sandals
p: Taking off a master's sandals was a slave's job. John says he is not fit even for that.
b: A later rabbinic saying holds that a disciple should do for his teacher every service a slave does, except untie his sandals, which was too degrading (Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 96a). John goes lower still: he is not worthy to do even a slave's work for the one who is coming. Luke omits Mark's "bend down" (Mark 1:7), and Paul's speech in Acts uses the saying again (Acts 13:25).

a: in the Holy Spirit and fire
p: Fire may mean judgment, as in 3:17, or cleansing, or the tongues of fire at Pentecost. Luke may intend all three.
b: Three readings: (1) Judgment: the next verse burns chaff with fire no one can put out, so the coming one brings the Spirit to the repentant and fire to the rest. (2) Cleansing: the fire refines, as in Malachi 3:2–3 and Isaiah 4:4, where God washes Zion "with a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning." (3) Pentecost: Luke's second volume fulfills the promise when tongues "like fire" rest on the disciples (Acts 2:3); the risen Jesus quotes John's words in Acts 1:5: "John baptized in water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit" (Acts 1:5). Some scholars think John himself said only "fire" or only "wind and fire" (Greek pneuma also means wind, and winnowing needs wind). Whether Spirit baptism is a second experience after conversion is set out on the cards at Acts 2 and Acts 8.
r: 3:17; Malachi 3:2–3; Isaiah 4:4; Acts 1:5; Acts 2:3; Acts 11:16; Acts 8:14–17; 12:49

p: The farmer tosses threshed grain into the wind with a fork. The heavy grain falls; the wind carries the chaff away.
b: A winnowing fork was a wooden pitchfork. After oxen had trampled the stalks, the farmer threw the mix into the evening breeze on an open threshing floor. Grain fell back, chaff blew aside and was swept up and burned. The prophets used the scene for God's judgment on the wicked (Psalm 1:4; Isaiah 41:15–16; Jeremiah 15:7). John's "coming one" is the farmer who already has the fork in hand, so sorting is near.

a: he kept telling the people the good news
t: John's fierce preaching as good news
p: Luke calls John's warnings "good news." The verb euangelizomai is one of Luke's favorite words; Mark never uses it.
b: Luke uses the verb ten times in the Gospel and fifteen in Acts. Here it covers a message that included vipers, axes and fire. For Luke, the announcement that God is coming to set things right is good news, even when it calls for hard change. Hans Conzelmann argued that Luke placed John in the old era of "the Law and the Prophets" (16:16), separate from the time of Jesus; this verse, in which John already brings the good news, is one reason many scholars think Conzelmann drew the line too sharply.

p: Antipas divorced his first wife to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother. John condemned it.
b: Josephus says Herodias was first married to a half-brother of Antipas whom he calls Herod; Mark calls him Philip (Mark 6:17), not the tetrarch of 3:1. Antipas divorced his first wife, a daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV, to marry her. The Law forbids marrying a brother's wife while the brother lives (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle (AD 36), and Josephus reports that many Jews saw the defeat as God's punishment for killing John (Antiquities 18.109–119). Luke tells the story briefly; Mark tells it in full (Mark 6:17–29). The KJV reads "his brother Philip's wife" from a later text (see the variant).

a: he shut John away in prison
p: Luke reports John's arrest before Jesus' baptism, and then never says who baptized Jesus.
b: Mark and Matthew tell of the arrest later (Mark 6:17; Matthew 14:3). Luke finishes John's story first, then tells of Jesus' baptism with a passive verb, "Jesus had been baptized" (3:21). Scholars read this in two ways. Many see Luke's tidy method of finishing one character before beginning the next (he does the same with Mary in 1:56). Others, following Conzelmann, think Luke wanted to mark off John's era from Jesus' and to avoid suggesting that Jesus was John's disciple. Luke does not deny that John baptized Jesus. Josephus says John was held at Machaerus, Herod's fortress east of the Dead Sea.

p: Only Luke says Jesus was praying when heaven opened. Luke shows him praying at every turning point.
b: Luke adds prayer to scene after scene: before choosing the Twelve (6:12), before Peter's confession (9:18), at the transfiguration (9:28–29), before teaching the Lord's Prayer (11:1), on the Mount of Olives (22:41–44) and on the cross (23:34, 46). He also notes Jesus' habit of slipping away to pray (5:16). In Acts the Spirit comes on the church while they pray (Acts 1:14; 2:1–4; 4:31). Luke's readers learn that the Spirit is given to those who ask (11:13).

p: Mark says Jesus saw the heavens "tearing open." Luke uses the ordinary verb "opened" and tells it as a public event.
b: Isaiah prayed, "If only you would rip open the heavens and come down" (Isaiah 64:1), and Ezekiel saw "the heavens opened" before his visions (Ezekiel 1:1). Mark's "tearing" (schizō) points ahead to the curtain torn at Jesus' death (Mark 15:38); Luke's "opened" (anoigō) matches the heavens Stephen sees opened (Acts 7:56) and Peter's vision (Acts 10:11). Mark and Matthew tell it from Jesus' point of view ("he saw"); Luke reports it as something that happened, though only Jesus is addressed.

a: in bodily shape, like a dove
p: Only Luke says the Spirit came "in bodily shape." Why a dove is debated.
b: Luke stresses that the event was real and visible. The dove has been read as: the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2; a later rabbi, Ben Zoma, compared the Spirit there to a dove hovering over her young, Babylonian Talmud, Hagigah 15a), so this is a new creation; the dove Noah sent out, bringing word of a renewed world after judgment (Genesis 8:8–12); Israel pictured as a dove (Hosea 11:11; Psalm 74:19); or simply gentleness. The Greek "like a dove" may describe the shape or the manner of coming down. Luke's interest in the bodily is lifelong: at the end the risen Jesus insists that he has flesh and bones (24:39).
orig: σωματικῷ εἴδει ὡς περιστεράν (sōmatikō eidei hōs peristeran)

p: The voice combines Psalm 2's king, Isaiah 42's servant and Isaac, Abraham's "only one, whom you love."
b: "You are my son" opens God's decree to the king in Psalm 2:7. "Dearly loved" (agapētos) is the Greek Old Testament's word for Isaac in Genesis 22:2, Abraham's son "whom you love." "In you I take delight" echoes the servant on whom God puts his Spirit: "my soul is pleased with him" (Isaiah 42:1). So the voice names Jesus as royal Son, beloved son offered by his father, and Spirit-filled servant. The words match Mark 1:11 exactly in the Greek. Some old witnesses give the voice the whole of Psalm 2:7 instead; see the variant.
orig: ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός (ho huios mou ho agapētos)

p: Thirty was the age of Joseph before Pharaoh and David as king. Luke says "about," and the dates allow a few years more.
b: Joseph was thirty when he entered Pharaoh's service (Genesis 41:46), David when he became king (2 Samuel 5:4), and Levites began full service at thirty (Numbers 4:3). Luke may want those echoes. If Jesus was born before Herod died in 4 BC (1:5; Matthew 2:1) and began work about AD 28, he was in his early thirties. Irenaeus, reasoning from "You are not even fifty" (John 8:57), thought Jesus taught into his forties (Against Heresies 2.22.5–6); few follow him.

p: The Greek says only "beginning." Luke means the beginning of his public work, as Acts says.
b: The participle archomenos has no object. English versions supply "his ministry" or "his work." Acts uses the same language: the apostles' witness must reach back to John's baptizing (Acts 1:22), and the message spread "beginning in Galilee" (Acts 10:37). Luke marks the start of the story the apostles would later testify to.

a: People supposed he was Joseph's son
p: Luke has just told of the virgin birth (1:34–35), so he adds that Jesus was only thought to be Joseph's son.
b: Hōs enomizeto, "as was supposed," is Luke's way of keeping his birth story while giving a family line through Joseph. In Jewish law a man who accepted a child as his own made him his legal heir; Joseph's line was therefore Jesus' line for purposes of descent. Matthew does something similar in his own way: "Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary" (Matthew 1:16), with a change of wording for Jesus. Some interpreters read the parenthesis differently, as a hint that the line that follows is Mary's (see the next note).

a: Joseph was the son of Heli
t: Heli or Jacob? Two family trees
p: Matthew makes Joseph the son of Jacob; Luke, of Heli. From David down, the two lists share almost no names.
b: Luke's list runs from Jesus back to God; Matthew's from Abraham forward to Jesus. Between David and Joseph they meet only at Shealtiel and Zerubbabel. Explanations: (1) Julius Africanus (about AD 221) proposed a levirate marriage: Heli died childless and his half-brother Jacob married the widow, so Joseph was Jacob's son by birth and Heli's by law (quoted in Eusebius, Church History 1.7). (2) Many since the 1400s, especially Protestants, read Luke's list as Mary's line, with Heli her father and Joseph his son-in-law. (3) Matthew gives the royal line of legal heirs, Luke the natural descent. (4) Most critical scholars think each writer drew on or built a different list for theological reasons, and that neither can now be checked. The chapter page sets these out.

p: Readers of the KJV meet several different names in this list. Most are only English spellings; a few come from a different Greek text.
b: The Byzantine text, which the KJV follows, has Ianna (KJV "Janna") for Jannai at 3:24; Semei for Semein, Iōsēph ("Joseph") for Josech and Iouda ("Juda") for Joda at 3:26; Mainan ("Menan") for Menna at 3:31; and "Aram" for Admin and Arni at 3:33 (see the variant). "Joseph" at 3:26 is a different name, not a spelling, probably the familiar name replacing the rare one. Other KJV forms are only older English spellings of the same Greek: Esrom (Hezron), Phalec (Peleg), Saruch (Serug), Ragau (Reu), Heber (Eber). The Plain English Translation follows the critical text and spells Old Testament names as the Plain English Translation of the Old Testament does.

a: the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel
p: Zerubbabel led the first return from Babylon. Both Gospels list him and his father Shealtiel, then go separate ways.
b: Zerubbabel, governor of Judah under Persia, rebuilt the altar and the temple (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1; 2:23). Ezra and Haggai call him the son of Shealtiel; 1 Chronicles 3:19 makes him the son of Shealtiel's brother Pedaiah, perhaps by levirate law. Matthew makes Shealtiel the son of King Jeconiah (Matthew 1:12); Luke makes him the son of Neri. Those who read Luke's list as Mary's line point to Jeremiah 22:30, where no offspring of Jeconiah will sit on David's throne, and suggest that Luke's line avoids that curse; others note that Haggai 2:23 seems to reverse it for Zerubbabel. Some scholars think the two Gospels mean two different men with the same names.
r: Matthew 1:12; 1 Chronicles 3:17–19; Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1; Haggai 2:23; Jeremiah 22:30

p: The Greek name here is Iēsous, the same as Jesus. Hebrew Yehoshua became Iēsous in Greek.
b: "Jesus" is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua or Yehoshua, "the LORD saves." Moses' successor Joshua is called Iēsous in the Greek Old Testament and in Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8. English Bibles write "Joshua" for these other men to avoid confusion, so this site does too. The Byzantine manuscripts read Iōsē (Jose) instead.

a: the son of Nathan, the son of David
p: Matthew traces the line through Solomon and the kings. Luke goes through Nathan, another son born to David in Jerusalem.
b: Nathan was one of the sons born to David and Bathsheba in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:14; 1 Chronicles 3:5); he is not Nathan the prophet. Zechariah 12:12 mentions "the family of the house of Nathan" among the mourners of Jerusalem. Luke's line is royal by descent from David but bypasses every king after him. Some read this as deliberate: the promised Son of David does not come through the line that failed. Others see no theological point and suppose Luke simply used a family list from Nathan's branch.

p: Matthew starts with Abraham. Luke runs on past him, through the ancestors of every nation, to Adam.
b: From Abraham back to Adam, Luke follows the lists of Genesis 5 and 11 (or 1 Chronicles 1:1–28) in the Greek Old Testament. Matthew's Jesus is first "son of David, son of Abraham" (Matthew 1:1), the heir of Israel's promises. Luke's Jesus belongs to all humanity, which fits Simeon's "a light to bring revelation to the nations" (2:32) and the Gentile mission of Acts.

t: The Cainan who is missing from Genesis
p: The Hebrew of Genesis 11 has no Cainan between Arpachshad and Shelah. The Greek Old Testament does, and Luke follows it.
b: In the Hebrew text, "Arpachshad lived 35 years and fathered Shelah" (Genesis 11:12). The Septuagint has "Arphaxad fathered Cainan, and Cainan fathered Sala," with ages for Cainan, and so does Jubilees 8:1–5, which tells of Cainan finding the Watchers' writings. Luke, who reads the Greek Bible, includes him. Nearly all manuscripts of Luke have the name; Codex Bezae leaves it out, and so perhaps does P75 (see the variant). It is a clear case of Luke's dependence on the Septuagint. Arphaxad is the Greek form of Arpachshad, and the Cainan of 3:37 is Genesis' Kenan (Genesis 5:9–14).

a: the son of Adam, the son of God
p: The list ends with God, Adam's maker. The next scene opens with the devil saying, "If you are God's Son."
b: Adam had no human father, so Luke calls him God's son; the Greek has only the article ("the of God") for every link, so "son" is understood. The genealogy sits between the voice at the baptism, "You are my dearly loved Son" (3:22), and the devil's "If you are God's Son" (4:3). Many readers see a new Adam story: the first son of God was tested in a garden over food and fell; this one is tested in the wilderness over food and stands. Paul makes the Adam comparison openly (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:45). Some scholars think Luke means less than that and simply ends the line with its source in God.

p: Luke's Spirit theme: the Spirit comes down in 3:22, fills Jesus here, empowers him in 4:14 and anoints him in 4:18.
b: Only Luke says "full of the Holy Spirit" before the testing. He uses the same phrase in Acts for Stephen and Barnabas (Acts 6:5; 7:55; 11:24), and "filled with the Holy Spirit" for John, Elizabeth, Zechariah and the apostles (1:15, 41, 67; Acts 2:4). The four mentions of the Spirit in 3:22–4:18 make a chain: the Spirit comes, fills, empowers and anoints. Luke wants his readers to see that the life of the church in Acts follows the pattern of Jesus' own life.

a: kept leading him about in the wilderness
t: Led in the wilderness, not just into it
p: The Spirit led Jesus "in" the wilderness for forty days, as God led Israel forty years in the wilderness.
b: Mark says the Spirit threw Jesus out into the wilderness, and Matthew that he was led up into it. Luke's Greek (ēgeto ... en tē erēmō) has a continuing verb and "in," so the Spirit was guiding him throughout the forty days of testing. The Byzantine text and the KJV read "into." The wording recalls Moses' words: "the LORD your God has led you on these forty years in the wilderness" (Deuteronomy 8:2), to humble and test Israel. All three of Jesus' answers come from Deuteronomy 6–8, Moses' sermon about those years.
orig: ἤγετο ἐν τῷ πνεύματι ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ (ēgeto en tō pneumati en tē erēmō)

a: while the devil put him to the test
p: Peirazō means "test" or "tempt." Luke says the testing went on through all forty days, then three tests came at the end.
b: The verb covers both a trial of character and an enticement to sin; English versions choose "tempt" or "test." This site says "test," as at Matthew 4:1, because the scene is a proving of the Son before his work begins, like Israel's testing in the wilderness. Diabolos, "devil," means "slanderer" and translates the Hebrew satan, "accuser," in the Greek Old Testament (Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1). Luke uses both names (4:8 in some manuscripts; 10:18; 22:3, 31).
orig: πειραζόμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ διαβόλου (peirazomenos hypo tou diabolou)

p: The Greek assumes the point for argument's sake: "since you are God's Son." The test is how he will use it.
b: The devil picks up the voice of 3:22 and the end of the genealogy (3:38). The grammar (a first-class condition, ei with the indicative) treats the statement as true for argument's sake. The devil is not asking Jesus to prove he is the Son; he is inviting him to use his sonship for himself: to feed himself, to grab the world, to force God's hand. The same taunt returns at the cross: "If you are the King of the Jews, save yourself" (23:37, 39).
orig: Εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ θεοῦ (Ei huios ei tou theou)

a: People will not live by bread alone
p: Moses told Israel that God fed them manna so they would learn that "people do not live by bread alone."
b: The full verse in Deuteronomy says God let Israel go hungry and fed them with manna "to teach you that people do not live by bread alone. People live by everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth." Jesus, hungry in the wilderness like Israel, chooses trust over self-help. The oldest manuscripts of Luke quote only the first half; later ones fill in the rest from Matthew 4:4 (see the variant). The "people" (ho anthrōpos, literally "the human being") are humanity in general.

a: every kingdom of the inhabited world
t: The inhabited world: the Roman Empire
p: Luke's word oikoumenē, "the inhabited world," is the word for the empire whose census opened the Gospel (2:1).
b: Matthew says "the world" (kosmos) and places the test on a very high mountain. Luke has no mountain in the oldest text (the Byzantine text adds one from Matthew; see the variant) and uses oikoumenē, the regular Greek term for the civilized world under Rome (2:1; Acts 11:28; 17:6; 24:5). For Luke's readers the offer sounds like the empire itself, whose rulers he listed in 3:1. "In a split second" (literally "a point of time") suggests a vision rather than a view from a height.
orig: πάσας τὰς βασιλείας τῆς οἰκουμένης (pasas tas basileias tēs oikoumenēs)

a: it has been handed over to me
t: Does the devil own the world?
p: Only Luke records this claim. Is it a lie, or does the devil really hold power over the kingdoms?
b: Readers differ. (1) A lie: the devil is "a liar and the father of falsehood" (John 8:44), and God rules the kingdoms of the world and gives them to whom he wills (Daniel 4:17, 32). (2) A partial truth: the New Testament calls Satan "this world's ruler" (John 12:31; 14:30), "the god of this age" (2 Corinthians 4:4), and says "the world, all of it, lies in the evil one's hands" (1 John 5:19); in Revelation 13:2 the dragon gives the beast his power and throne. On this reading, the devil's authority is real but borrowed and temporary. Jesus does not dispute the claim; he refuses the price. Luke later shows the risen Jesus receiving authority from God, not from the devil (24:26, 49; Acts 2:36).
r: John 8:44; John 12:31; 2 Corinthians 4:4; 1 John 5:19; Daniel 4:17; Revelation 13:2; 10:18–19; 11:21–22

p: Proskyneō means bowing low to the ground before someone. It is also the Greek word for worship.
b: This site renders proskyneō "bow down" in the Gospels, because the word names a bodily act: kneeling and touching the forehead to the ground before a king, a master or a god. The same act could be simple respect or worship; the Gospel leaves the reader to judge who deserves it. Here the devil demands it, and Jesus' answer from Deuteronomy restricts it to God. At the end of Luke the disciples bow down before the risen Jesus (24:52).

a: It is the Lord your God you must bow down to
p: The Hebrew says "fear." Jesus' Greek says "bow down to" and adds "alone."
b: The Hebrew of Deuteronomy 6:13 reads: "It is the LORD your God you must fear." Most manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament also have "fear" (so Codex Vaticanus, and the text Rahlfs prints); Codex Alexandrinus has "bow down to" and "alone," probably under the Gospels' influence. The Gospels' "bow down to" and "alone" (monō) sharpen the answer to the devil's demand. The words are the same as Matthew 4:10. The Byzantine text, followed by the KJV, adds "Get behind me, Satan," from Matthew (see the variant).

p: The Greek pterygion, "little wing," is some high edge of the temple. Its exact spot is unknown.
b: Candidates are the southeast corner of the Temple Mount, where the Royal Porch towered over the Kidron Valley (Josephus says looking down from it made one dizzy, Antiquities 15.411–412), or a lintel or turret over a gate. A second-century story told by Hegesippus has James the brother of Jesus thrown down from the "wing of the temple" (in Eusebius, Church History 2.23). Matthew calls Jerusalem "the holy city"; Luke names it.

a: Then he took him into Jerusalem
p: Matthew's order is bread, temple, mountain. Luke's is bread, kingdoms, temple, so the tests end in Jerusalem.
b: Most scholars think the source had one order and one Gospel changed it. Matthew's order climbs to a mountain, where his Gospel also ends (Matthew 28:16), and finishes with "Go away, Satan!" Luke's order ends at the temple in Jerusalem, the city where his Gospel begins and ends (1:9; 24:53), toward which Jesus will "set his face" (9:51), and where the devil will return through Judas (22:3). Some also see the order of Psalm 106 or of Israel's wilderness tests; there is no agreement. Either way the three answers come from Deuteronomy. In Matthew's order they run backward through Moses' sermon (8:3, then 6:16, then 6:13); Luke's order (8:3, 6:13, 6:16) breaks that pattern, which some take as a sign that Matthew kept the source's order.

p: Psalm 91 promises angels to guard the one who trusts God. The devil quotes it to urge a stunt.
b: The devil now uses Scripture, Psalm 91:11–12 in the Greek. Luke's quotation is a little longer than Matthew's (it keeps "to guard you"), but it still leaves off the end of the line, "to guard you on every road you take" (Psalm 91:11): the promise is for the path God gives, not for a leap God never asked for. The psalm goes on to say the protected one will tread on lion and snake (Psalm 91:13); Jesus later gives his disciples authority to tread on snakes and scorpions (10:19).

a: You must not put the Lord your God to the test
p: Israel at Massah demanded water to prove God was with them. Jesus refuses to make God prove himself.
b: Deuteronomy 6:16 says, "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16). At Massah the people said, "Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?" (Exodus 17:7). Throwing himself down would be the same demand turned into a show. Luke introduces it with "It has been said" instead of "It is written," perhaps to vary the formula. Some readers also hear a second sense: the devil must not test Jesus, who is "the Lord"; most scholars think the first sense is Luke's main point.

t: When does the devil come back?
p: The devil leaves "until a fitting time" (kairos). Luke next names Satan entering Judas (22:3).
b: Achri kairou means "until a suitable time." Hans Conzelmann argued that Luke pictures Jesus' ministry as a "Satan-free" period between 4:13 and 22:3. Most scholars now disagree: Jesus fights demons throughout, sees Satan fall (10:18), says the bent woman was bound by Satan (13:16), and calls his disciples those who stayed with him in his trials (22:28). Luke's point is that the contest is not over; the decisive "time" comes at the Passion, when Jesus says, "this hour belongs to you, and to the authority of darkness" (22:53).
orig: ἄχρι καιροῦ (achri kairou), 'until a suitable time'

p: Luke pairs "Spirit" and "power" from the annunciation (1:35) to Pentecost (Acts 1:8).
b: The angel told Mary the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High would come on her (1:35); the risen Jesus promises the disciples power when the Spirit comes (24:49; Acts 1:8). Peter sums up Jesus' life with the same pair, "how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power" (Acts 10:38). Here, after the testing, the Spirit who led Jesus in the wilderness sends him back to Galilee to begin.

p: Synagogues were meeting houses where villagers gathered on the Sabbath to hear the Law read and explained.
b: Archaeologists have found first-century synagogue buildings at Magdala (excavated from 2009, with a carved stone table showing the temple menorah), Gamla and elsewhere, and a Greek inscription from Jerusalem records that Theodotus built a synagogue "for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments." Such buildings were also village halls. A traveling teacher could be invited to read and speak, as Jesus does here and Paul does in Acts 13:15. On "glorify" (doxazō), here "spoke of him with honor," compare the crowds praising God in 5:25–26.

t: A Jew at his synagogue on the Sabbath
p: Luke stresses that Jesus went to the synagogue every Sabbath, as was his custom.
b: The phrase kata to eiōthos, "according to his custom," is used again of Paul going into the synagogue at Thessalonica (Acts 17:2). Luke presents Jesus, his family and the first Christians as faithful Jews: circumcised on the eighth day (2:21), presented at the temple "as the Law of the Lord says" (2:22–24, 39), worshiping at the feasts (2:41), and resting on the Sabbath at his burial (23:56). Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine stress that Luke's Jesus is at home in synagogue life, not opposed to it.
orig: κατὰ τὸ εἰωθὸς αὐτῷ (kata to eiōthos autō)

p: A first-century Sabbath gathering included reading from the Law, then from the Prophets, and teaching.
b: Our earliest detailed rules come from the Mishnah (about AD 200), which describes readers standing to read the Torah and a passage from the Prophets (the haftarah), and allows the reader of the Prophets to skip from place to place, though not in the Torah (Mishnah Megillah 4:1–4). Acts 13:15 mentions "the reading of the Law and the Prophets" followed by a word of encouragement. It is debated whether there was already a fixed cycle of readings in Jesus' time; Luke's "found the spot" may mean Jesus chose the passage. The reader stood; the teacher sat (4:20).

a: The Spirit of the Lord is on me
t: Isaiah 61, with a line from Isaiah 58
p: Jesus reads Isaiah 61:1–2 in its Greek form, adds a line from 58:6, and stops before "the day of vengeance."
b: Three changes stand out. (1) A line is missing: the oldest manuscripts of Luke lack Isaiah's "to bandage the broken in heart" (Isaiah 61:1), which later copies restore (see the variant). (2) A line is added from Isaiah 58:6, God's description of a true fast: "to send the crushed away free" (Isaiah 58:6). (3) The reading stops in mid-sentence, before "and a day of our God's vengeance" (Isaiah 61:2). The Greek also has "sight again for the blind" where the Hebrew has "an opening wide for those who are bound" (Isaiah 61:1). Luke's summary is release, healing and welcome. Christian readers have long seen the vengeance held over for the second coming; others see judgment set aside in favor of mercy.

p: "Anointed" is echrisen, from the same root as Christos. Jesus claims to be the Spirit-anointed one of Isaiah.
b: Chriō, "anoint," is the verb behind Christos, "anointed one," the Greek for mashiach, Messiah. Kings and priests were anointed with oil; in Isaiah 61 the speaker is anointed with the Spirit for a prophetic task. Luke connects the anointing with the Spirit's coming at the baptism, as Peter later does: "how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power" (Acts 10:38). The early church prayed about "Jesus, your holy servant, whom you anointed" (Acts 4:27).

a: to bring good news to the poor
p: Luke means people who are actually poor, but the word also carried the sense of the humble who depend on God.
b: Isaiah's Hebrew anavim means the afflicted or humble; the Greek ptōchoi means the destitute, beggars. Luke keeps both senses in view. His Gospel is full of the materially poor and of warnings to the rich (1:53; 6:20–24; 14:13, 21; 16:19–31). Readings differ: many Catholic and Protestant interpreters stress the spiritually poor who rely on God, as in Matthew 5:3; liberation theologians such as Gustavo Gutiérrez read Luke 4 as a program of release for the poor and oppressed; others combine them. Luke's own answer comes in 7:22, where healings and good news to the poor show that Jesus is the one who was to come. See the topic page on poverty and the Beatitudes at 6:20.

p: Aphesis, "release," is the Greek Bible's word for the jubilee year and also Luke's word for forgiveness of sins.
b: In the Greek of Leviticus 25:10 the jubilee is "a year of release" (aphesis), when debts were cancelled, land returned and Israelite slaves freed. Isaiah 61 draws on that picture, and Luke's quotation uses aphesis twice: "release to the captives" and the crushed sent "away free" (literally "in release"). Luke uses the same noun for the forgiveness of sins (3:3; 24:47). Whether Jesus meant a literal social release, a spiritual forgiveness, or both is discussed at 4:19.

a: a year of the Lord's welcome
t: The year of the Lord's welcome: a real jubilee?
p: Isaiah's "year of the LORD's goodwill" echoes the jubilee. A program to practice, or God's age of salvation?
b: Dektos means "welcome, acceptable"; the year is the time when God shows favor. Readings: (1) a literal program: John Howard Yoder and Sharon Ringe argued that Jesus proclaimed a real jubilee, with debts forgiven and the poor restored, to be lived by his followers; (2) an image of the messianic age, when God sets captives free from sin, sickness and the devil, with social consequences but no legal program; (3) both. There is no clear evidence that the jubilee of Leviticus 25 was ever kept in Second Temple times. At Qumran, 11QMelchizedek joined Isaiah 61 to the jubilee laws and pictured a heavenly deliverer proclaiming release in the last jubilee. Pope John Paul II linked Luke 4 to the Christian jubilee of 2000, with a call to reduce the debts of poor nations.

p: The hypēretēs was the synagogue's attendant, who kept the scrolls and handed them to readers.
b: Later Jewish sources call him the chazzan. He brought out the scroll from its chest and put it back after the reading. Jesus sits down to teach, the normal posture of a teacher (5:3; Matthew 5:1). The eyes "locked on him" (atenizō, a favorite word of Luke in Acts) show the suspense before the shortest sermon in the Bible.

p: "Today" is Luke's word for the arrival of salvation: born today, fulfilled today, salvation today, paradise today.
b: The angel tells the shepherds, "For today a Savior was born for you in David's town" (2:11); here Scripture is fulfilled today; the crowd says, "We have seen things past believing today" (5:26); Jesus tells Zacchaeus, "Today salvation has come to this household" (19:9), and the criminal, "today you will be with me in paradise" (23:43). For Luke the promises are not only for the end of time. The sermon's one recorded sentence claims that the Isaiah passage is now happening in the person reading it. "In your ears" is a Hebrew way of saying "as you listen."

a: Everyone was speaking in his favor
p: The Greek says "they were all testifying to him." Most read it as praise; a few read it as testifying against him.
b: Emartyroun autō normally means "bore witness for him," that is, spoke well of him. Joachim Jeremias argued that the dative could mean "against him": the hearers were angry that Jesus stopped before "the day of vengeance" on Israel's enemies, and "words of grace" means words of mercy alone. Most scholars keep the positive sense: the mood turns at Jesus' next words, as it does in many of Luke's scenes, when admiration meets a claim the hearers will not accept. "Words of grace" (logoi tēs charitos) can mean gracious, charming speech or words about God's grace; Luke may intend both.

a: This is Joseph's son, isn't it?
t: Luke's version of the hometown visit
p: Mark and Matthew tell of Jesus rejected at home midway through his work. Luke puts it first, as a program.
b: Mark 6:1–6 and Matthew 13:53–58 share the question about Jesus' family and the saying about a prophet at home. Most scholars think Luke rewrote Mark's scene, joined it to the Isaiah reading and moved it to the front of the Gospel as an overture: anointed by the Spirit, Jesus brings release, is rejected by his own, speaks of God's care for outsiders, and escapes death. One clue to the move is 4:23, which mentions deeds at Capernaum that Luke has not yet told. Others think Luke had a separate tradition of an early visit to Nazareth ("Proto-Luke").

p: The saying was known in Greek and Jewish sources: a doctor should first heal his own sickness.
b: Similar sayings appear in Greek literature and in a rabbinic midrash (Genesis Rabbah 23:4, "Physician, physician, heal your own limp"), as commentators such as Fitzmyer note. Here the townspeople mean: do for your own town what you did for strangers. On the cross the rulers make the same demand, "Let him save himself" (23:35). Early tradition made Luke a physician (Colossians 4:14), and readers have enjoyed a doctor reporting this proverb.

a: no prophet is welcome in his hometown
p: The word dektos, "welcome," is the one Jesus just read in "a year of the Lord's welcome" (4:19).
b: Matthew and Mark say a prophet is "without honor" at home (Matthew 13:57; Mark 6:4). Luke uses dektos instead, linking the saying to the reading: the prophet who announces God's welcome is not welcomed. The saying is also in John 4:44 and in the Gospel of Thomas 31. This is also Luke's first "Amen, I tell you," one of only six in his Gospel (he often prefers "Truly," alēthōs). Jews said "amen" at the end of a prayer to agree with it; Jesus put it first, to stress his own words. Joachim Jeremias argued that no one before him is known to have done this; others point to possible parallels and think the claim goes too far.

p: 1 Kings says the rain came back "in the third year." Luke and James say three years and six months.
b: 1 Kings 18:1 dates the end of the drought "in the third year" (counted from Elijah's stay with the widow, or from the start). Luke and James 5:17 both say three and a half years, which suggests a Jewish tradition known to both. Three and a half years, half of seven, had become a set period of distress in Daniel (Daniel 7:25; 12:7: "a time, times and half a time") and appears again in Revelation (Revelation 11:2–3; 12:6, 14).
r: 1 Kings 17:1; 1 Kings 18:1; James 5:17; Daniel 7:25; Daniel 12:7; Revelation 11:2–3; Revelation 12:6

t: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath
p: God told Elijah, "Go to Zarephath, a town of Sidon," to a foreign widow who fed him; he later raised her son.
b: Zarephath lay on the Phoenician coast between Tyre and Sidon, in Jezebel's home country (1 Kings 16:31). The LORD sent Elijah there, "Go to Zarephath, a town of Sidon" (1 Kings 17:9), to a Gentile widow, while Israel's widows went hungry. Luke tells a matching story soon after: Jesus raises the only son of a widow at Nain and "gave him to his mother" (7:15), the very words of 1 Kings 17:23, and the crowd calls him a great prophet (7:16).

t: Outsiders, and why the hometown was offended
p: Elijah and Elisha were sent to foreigners. Jesus uses Israel's own Scriptures to say God's care reaches beyond Israel.
b: Naaman, commander of the army of Aram (Syria), Israel's enemy, was healed of skin disease by Elisha (2 Kings 5:1–14); on "skin disease," which is not modern leprosy, see 5:12. Both examples are from the Scriptures Jesus' hearers revered. The point is not that God rejects Israel: Elijah and Elisha were Israel's prophets, and Israel's prophets often criticized their own people from the inside. But it does tell a town that wanted favors that God's prophets go where God sends them. Luke's second volume follows this pattern as the message goes to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46–48; 28:28). Readers should not turn the scene into a picture of "the Jews" rejecting Jesus: the hearers are one village, and the rest of Luke shows many Jews welcoming him.

p: Admiration turns into a lynch mob in seven verses. Interpreters give different reasons.
b: Suggested reasons: (1) Jesus refused to perform signs for his hometown on demand (4:23); (2) he implied that God's favor would pass to Gentiles like the widow and Naaman; (3) he claimed to be the anointed one of Isaiah, which seemed blasphemy from a local builder's son; (4) on Jeremias's reading, he left out vengeance on the nations (see 4:22). Luke repeats the pattern in Acts, where a synagogue's welcome turns to violent opposition when Paul turns to the Gentiles (Acts 13:42–50; 22:21–22). Scholars such as Jack T. Sanders read Luke-Acts as hostile to Jews; others, such as Jacob Jervell, argue that Luke shows Israel divided, with many Jews believing. Christians later used scenes like this against Jews; the text describes one town's anger, not a people's guilt.

a: the edge of the hill their town was built on
p: Nazareth lies in a basin on a hillside. The traditional "Mount of the Leap" is about two miles away.
b: First-century Nazareth was a small village of perhaps a few hundred people on the slopes of a hill in lower Galilee; houses and tombs from the period have been excavated. There are drops near the old village, and a cliff to the southeast, the Mount of Precipitation, has been shown to pilgrims since the Middle Ages. The Mishnah's later procedure for stoning began by pushing the condemned from a height (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:4), and some scholars think the crowd meant to begin a stoning; others see simple mob violence. Either way, the story foreshadows the city that will kill Jesus.

a: passed through the middle of them and kept going
p: Luke gives no explanation. Was it a miracle, the force of his presence, or simply that his time had not come?
b: Some readers see a miracle; others the authority that silences demons; Luke says nothing. The verb poreuomai, "go on one's way," is the word Jesus uses in 13:33 for the road that must lead him on to Jerusalem. Many scholars see the whole scene as a preview of the Gospel: proclaimed, rejected by his own, taken out to be killed, and yet going on. John records similar escapes (John 8:59; 10:39).

p: "Down" is literal: Nazareth is in the hills, Capernaum on the lakeshore about 700 feet below sea level.
b: Capernaum (Hebrew Kefar Nahum, "Nahum's village") lay on the northwest shore of the Lake of Galilee, near the border between Antipas' and Philip's lands, with a customs post (5:27). Excavations show a fishing town of basalt houses. Beneath a fifth-century octagonal church lies a house whose main room was plastered and used for gatherings from the first century, with Christian graffiti, which some scholars identify with Peter's house (4:38). The white limestone synagogue now visible is from the fourth or fifth century, built over an earlier basalt floor that may be from Jesus' day.

p: Mark contrasts Jesus' authority with the scribes'. Luke drops the contrast.
b: Mark 1:22 says he taught "as one who held authority, and not as the scribes did." Luke omits the scribes, perhaps because his Gentile readers would not know them yet, or because he avoids a polemical note before the scribes appear in 5:21. Henry Cadbury showed many such small changes: Luke smooths Mark's Greek, trims repetitions, and tones down harsh details. The word for "message" is logos, which Luke uses for Jesus' preaching and later for the apostles' (Acts 4:31).

a: the spirit of an unclean demon
p: In ordinary Greek a daimonion could be a neutral or even good spirit, so Luke specifies "unclean."
b: For many Greeks a daimonion was any divine being; Socrates spoke of his guiding daimonion, and Paul's Athenian hearers called him a herald of "foreign divinities" (daimonia, Acts 17:18). Jews used the word for evil spirits. Luke, writing for readers who knew both uses, makes it clear: this is an unclean, hostile spirit. "Unclean" uses the language of purity: the holy one of God meets impurity and drives it out.

p: Ea is a cry of surprise or anger. The KJV's "Let us alone" takes it as a command from the verb eaō, "let be."
b: Ea is an interjection found in Greek drama and in Job in the Greek Old Testament (Job 15:16; 25:6), expressing dismay or indignation, something like "Ha!" or "Ah!" The KJV followed earlier interpreters who read it as the command form of eaō, "leave alone." The two forms are spelled alike; most scholars take it as the interjection because it stands alone at the head of a cry, as in Job 15:16 and 25:6 in the Greek. Some manuscripts of Mark 1:24 also have the word (see the variant there).

p: The demon names Jesus with a title used of Aaron's line and later of Jesus in Acts.
b: Psalm 106:16 calls Aaron "the LORD's holy one." Peter calls Jesus "the Holy and Righteous One" (Acts 3:14), and the church prays about "Jesus, your holy servant" (Acts 4:27, 30). In the ancient world knowing a spirit's name gave power over it; the demon tries the same on Jesus, and fails. In Luke the angel had promised Mary that her child would be called holy (1:35).

p: Luke adds that the man was unharmed. In 1882 W. K. Hobart argued that such touches showed a physician's hand.
b: Hobart collected words in Luke-Acts that appear in Greek medical writers, such as the "high fever" of 4:38, and argued that the author was "Luke, the beloved doctor" (Colossians 4:14). Henry Cadbury replied in 1920 that the same words appear in non-medical writers like Josephus and Lucian, so the vocabulary proves only that Luke was an educated Greek writer. Most scholars now accept Cadbury's point, while many still think the traditional author could have been a doctor. The added detail here simply makes Jesus' authority complete: the demon leaves and can do no harm.

p: Luke mentions Simon here as if the reader knows him, before telling of his call in 5:1–11.
b: In Mark, Jesus calls Simon and Andrew (Mark 1:16–20) before healing Simon's mother-in-law (Mark 1:29–31). Luke moves the call later, after Simon has seen Jesus at work, which makes his obedience in 5:5 more natural. The scene also shows that Simon was married, as Paul confirms (1 Corinthians 9:5). Whether church leaders may marry is set out on the card at Matthew 8:14.

a: gave the fever a strict order
p: Jesus speaks to the fever with the same verb he uses for the demon (4:35) and the demons (4:41).
b: Epitimaō, "rebuke, give a strict order," is used in the Gospels for silencing demons and calming the storm (8:24). Luke uses it three times in a few verses: demon, fever, demons. Ancient people often thought of fevers as attacks by hostile powers, and Luke later calls a woman's illness bondage by Satan (13:16). He does not say the fever was a demon, but he treats it as an enemy that must obey.

p: Diakoneō is the verb for waiting on table and, in Luke, for discipleship itself.
b: The healed woman gets up "at once," a sign of a full cure, and serves the household. Some read only hospitality; others see the first of Luke's women who serve Jesus, like the women who "were serving them out of what they owned" (8:3) and Martha (10:40). Jesus says, "I, in your company, am like the one who waits on tables" (22:27), and the church's first deacons are appointed to "serve tables" (Acts 6:2).

t: Waiting for the Sabbath to end
p: The synagogue healing was on the Sabbath. People waited for sunset, when it ended, to carry their sick.
b: A Jewish day runs from sunset to sunset. Carrying burdens from one domain to another was forbidden on the Sabbath (Jeremiah 17:21–22; Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 lists carrying out among the main kinds of work), so the townspeople waited. Their care shows a community that kept the Sabbath. Luke does not criticize it here; disputes over healing on the Sabbath come later (6:6–11; 13:10–17; 14:1–6).

a: placed his hands on each of them
p: Luke stresses that Jesus touched every sick person one by one.
b: Mark says he healed "many"; Luke says he laid hands on "each one of them." Laying on of hands for healing appears again in 13:13 and in Acts, where Ananias lays hands on Saul and Paul on Publius' father (Acts 9:12, 17; 28:8). In Acts the same gesture also accompanies the giving of the Spirit and appointment to service (Acts 6:6; 8:17).

a: they knew him to be the Messiah
p: Luke explains the demons' cry "You are God's Son" as knowledge that he was the Messiah.
b: Mark 1:34 says only that the demons knew him. Luke spells it out, equating "God's Son" with "the Messiah" (ho christos), as he does in the angel's words (1:32–35) and at the trial (22:67–70). Why silence them? Luke does not stress the "messianic secret" as much as Mark, but here too Jesus will not accept testimony from demons, and his own way of being Messiah has to be learned (9:20–22).
orig: τὸν χριστὸν αὐτὸν εἶναι (ton christon auton einai)

p: The small Greek word dei, "it is necessary," marks things God has planned. Luke uses it often for Jesus' mission.
b: The boy Jesus "had to" be in his Father's house (2:49); the Son of Man "must" suffer (9:22; 17:25); Jesus "must" stay at Zacchaeus' house (19:5); everything written about him "had to" be fulfilled (24:44). Here the necessity is to move on: the good news is not for Capernaum alone. The crowds' attempt to keep Jesus contrasts with Nazareth's attempt to throw him out; both try to control him.

t: The kingdom of God, first mention
p: Luke's first use of the phrase at the center of Jesus' preaching. "Kingdom" also means "reign": God ruling as king.
b: Basileia means both a realm and the act of reigning. Jewish prayers and the Psalms celebrate God's kingship (Psalm 145:11–13; Daniel 2:44); Jesus announces that it is arriving in his work (11:20; 17:21) and will come in full at the end (21:31; 22:16–18). Matthew usually writes "kingdom of heaven"; Luke always says "kingdom of God." In Acts the apostles go on preaching the same kingdom (Acts 1:3; 28:31).
orig: τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ θεοῦ (tēn basileian tou theou)

p: Mark and Matthew call it "the Sea of Galilee." Luke, a Greek writer, calls it a lake, which is what it is.
b: The body of fresh water is about 13 miles long and 8 wide. Mark and Matthew follow the Hebrew habit of calling any large water a "sea" (yam), as in Numbers 34:11, "the Sea of Chinnereth." Luke always says limnē, "lake" (5:2; 8:22–23, 33), the normal Greek word. Gennesaret was the fertile plain on the northwest shore; 1 Maccabees 11:67 speaks of "the water of Gennesar," and Josephus describes the plain's fruitfulness (Jewish War 3.506–521). John calls the lake "the Sea of Tiberias" (John 21:1).
r: Numbers 34:11; Mark 1:16; Matthew 4:18; John 6:1; John 21:1; 1 Maccabees 11:67; 8:22–23

p: Luke's name for the message Jesus preached, and later for the message the apostles spread.
b: Luke uses "the word of God" for Jesus' preaching (5:1; 8:11, 21; 11:28) and, in Acts, for the apostles' message, which "kept growing" as the church grew (Acts 6:7; 12:24; 19:20). The crowd presses to hear it; Simon will soon act on Jesus' word (5:5). The phrase ties the Gospel to the prophets, to whom "the word of God" came, as it came to John in 3:2.

p: Fishermen worked through the night with large nets, then cleaned and mended them in the morning.
b: On the Lake of Galilee the main catch was taken at night, with a trammel net (a wall of layered nets) or a dragnet let down from boats. In the morning the nets were washed of weed and mud, dried and repaired. A boat from this period, found in the mud near Magdala in 1986, is about 27 feet long and could carry a crew of four or five and their catch. Simon's partners (5:7, 10) suggest a small family business like the one Mark describes with "hired workers" (Mark 1:20).

a: seated in the boat, he went on teaching the crowds
p: Pushing a little way out let Jesus speak to a crowd on the shore, whose sloping banks could act as a natural theater.
b: Mark has the same practice before the parables (Mark 4:1). Water carries sound, and the coves near Capernaum have sloping shores where a crowd could sit and hear a speaker in a boat. Sitting was the posture of a teacher (4:20). Luke turns the teaching into the setting of a call: the man whose boat became a pulpit is about to become a disciple.

p: Only Luke uses epistatēs for Jesus. It replaces "Rabbi" and "Teacher" in several parallel scenes.
b: Epistatēs was a general Greek word for a person in charge: a supervisor, a commander. Luke uses it in six scenes (seven times, since 8:24 has it twice), always from disciples or people asking for help (5:5; 8:24, 45; 9:33, 49; 17:13). Where Mark has the Aramaic "Rabbi" (Mark 9:5), Luke has "Master" (9:33), avoiding Semitic words his Greek readers might not know. Here Simon begins with "Master" and, after the catch, falls down and says "Lord" (5:8). Luke also writes "Master" for a different word, despotēs, "owner, sovereign," which Simeon uses of God (2:29); epistatēs is the word here, and Luke uses it only for Jesus.

a: on the strength of what you say, I will lower the nets
p: Experienced fishermen knew daylight in deep water was the wrong time. Simon obeys anyway.
b: Fish in this lake were caught mostly at night near the shore; a daytime cast in deep water made little sense to a professional. Simon's "on the strength of what you say" (literally "upon your saying," epi tō rhēmati sou) is the reply Luke wants from every hearer. Mary's "just as you have said" (1:38) renders the same noun: kata to rhēma sou, "according to your saying." Interpreters differ on whether Simon was trusting or merely humoring the teacher who had healed his mother-in-law; the outcome makes the point either way.

a: they trapped a great mass of fish
t: Luke 5 and John 21: one catch or two?
p: John 21 tells a very similar catch after the resurrection. Many scholars think the two go back to one event.
b: Shared features: a night of catching nothing, Jesus' command to let down the nets, a huge catch, the nets under strain, Peter's dramatic response, and a commission ("catching people" in Luke; "feed my sheep" in John). Views: (1) Two separate events; the second deliberately echoes the first, recalling Peter's call as he is restored after his denial. This is the traditional view and is still held by many. (2) One tradition: an appearance of the risen Jesus moved by Luke back into the ministry (as Raymond Brown and others argue), or a ministry story moved by John's tradition to after Easter. In Luke the nets were "starting to rip apart"; in John "still the net did not tear" (John 21:11), which some read as a deliberate contrast.

p: Simon reacts as Isaiah did in the temple: the closeness of the holy makes a person aware of sin.
b: Seeing God's glory, Isaiah cried, "Woe to me! I am finished" (Isaiah 6:5), because of unclean lips; Gideon and Manoah feared death after seeing the angel of the LORD (Judges 6:22; 13:22). Simon falls at Jesus' knees and asks him to go away. Jesus' answer, "Stop being afraid," and the commission that follows, match the pattern of prophetic call stories: fear, reassurance, sending. Luke here first calls him "Simon Peter"; Jesus gives him the name in 6:14. Simon also shifts from "Master" (5:5) to "Lord" (kyrie).

a: it is people you will be catching alive
p: The verb zōgreō means "take alive." Luke's image is of rescue, not of a fish caught to be eaten.
b: Mark and Matthew have "fishermen who catch people" (Mark 1:17; Matthew 4:19). Luke uses zōgreō, "capture alive," a word used in war for sparing captives (in the Greek of Numbers 31:15, 18 and Joshua 2:13; 6:25, of keeping people alive). In Jeremiah 16:16 God sends fishers and hunters to catch Israel for judgment; Luke's word turns the image toward saving life. The periphrastic future, "you will be catching," describes an ongoing task.
r: Mark 1:17; Matthew 4:19; Jeremiah 16:16; Numbers 31:15, 18; Joshua 6:25; 2 Timothy 2:26

a: they left it all behind and followed him
p: Only Luke says they left "everything." He repeats the word for Levi and in Jesus' demands.
b: Mark says they left their nets and their father (Mark 1:18, 20). Luke says "all," right after the biggest catch of their lives. Levi too "left everything" (5:28). Jesus later says that no one can be his disciple without giving up all he has (14:33), tells a ruler to sell everything (18:22), and hears Peter say that they have left their own things to follow him (18:28). How literally to take this has divided Christians: monastic tradition took it as a call for some; most churches read it as a call to put Christ above possessions. See the card at Matthew 19:21.

a: a man full of skin disease
p: Not leprosy in the modern sense. And in the Law a person whose skin was fully covered could be declared clean.
b: Lepra translates the Hebrew tsara'at, a range of skin conditions that made a person ritually unclean (Leviticus 13–14). It was not Hansen's disease, which may not have reached the region until later; this site says "skin disease." Luke alone says the man was "full of" it, which can mean a severe case. Leviticus contains a surprising rule: "If the skin disease has covered his whole body, he is to declare the person clean" (Leviticus 13:13). Luke probably means only that the illness was advanced; the man still begs to be made clean.

p: Touching a person with skin disease made one unclean. Here the contact goes the other way.
b: The Law told the sufferer to live apart: "He is to live alone, and his home is to be outside the camp" (Leviticus 13:46). Uncleanness was not sin; it was a temporary state that kept a person from the temple and was removed by waiting, washing and offerings. Jewish scholars such as Paula Fredriksen and Amy-Jill Levine warn against picturing the purity laws as cruelty that Jesus came to abolish: Jesus sends the man to the priest (5:14). The story's point is power: instead of Jesus becoming unclean, the man becomes clean.

t: Back to the priest, as Moses ordered
p: The Law gave the priest the task of confirming the cure and offering the sacrifices of cleansing.
b: Leviticus 14 lays out the procedure: "He is to be brought to the priest" (Leviticus 14:2), who examines him outside the camp, then a ceremony with two birds, washing, shaving and, on the eighth day, offerings at the sanctuary. In Jesus' time this meant a trip to the temple in Jerusalem. Jesus upholds the Law and sends the man back into the community through its proper door. "As evidence to them" may mean proof to the priests that the man was cured, a witness to them about Jesus, or (less likely) evidence against them; Mark has the same phrase (Mark 1:44).

a: Yet talk about him traveled farther than ever
p: Mark says the healed man disobeyed and spread the story. Luke leaves him out: the news simply spread.
b: In Mark 1:45 the man "went out and started preaching it far and wide," so that Jesus could no longer enter towns openly. Luke omits the man's disobedience and the restriction. This is typical of the way Luke trims Mark: fewer failures by minor characters, and the crowds' growing interest in place of Jesus' enforced retreat.

a: kept slipping away to the wild places and praying there
p: The Greek describes a repeated habit: the busier Jesus became, the more often he withdrew to pray.
b: The construction ēn hypochōrōn ... kai proseuchomenos, "he was withdrawing and praying," marks a regular practice, not one occasion. "The wild places" (hai erēmoi) are the same wilderness where he was tested (4:1). Luke sets this verse between growing crowds and growing opposition. See 3:21 on Luke's theme of prayer.
orig: ἦν ὑποχωρῶν ... καὶ προσευχόμενος (ēn hypochōrōn ... kai proseuchomenos)

a: Pharisees and teachers of the law
p: The Pharisees appear here for the first time in Luke. His portrait of them is mixed, not simply hostile.
b: The Pharisees were a popular lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law, including purity and tithing, and to the "traditions of the elders." "Teachers of the law" (nomodidaskaloi) is a rare word; Luke uses it again of Gamaliel, a Pharisee who defends the apostles (Acts 5:34). Luke's Pharisees criticize Jesus, but they also invite him to dinner (7:36; 11:37; 14:1), warn him of Herod's plot (13:31), and in Acts some become believers (Acts 15:5) and defend Paul (Acts 23:9). Paul calls himself a Pharisee (Acts 23:6). Jewish historians stress that Pharisaic teaching shaped the rabbinic Judaism that followed. Here they come "from every village" to see for themselves.

p: "The Lord" here is God. Luke says God's power was present, so Jesus healed.
b: Luke often speaks of power (dynamis) going out from Jesus (6:19; 8:46) and of the Spirit's power (4:14). Here he attributes it to "the Lord," meaning God, as in the Greek Old Testament. The verse prepares for the question of who can forgive sins: the healing that follows shows the Lord at work. The manuscripts differ over whether the power was there "for him to heal" or "to heal them"; see the variant.

p: Mark says they dug through the roof, as you would through a mud roof. Luke says they went through the tiles.
b: Houses in Capernaum had flat roofs of beams covered with branches and packed mud, reached by an outside stair. Mark's men "unroofed the roof" and "dug an opening" (Mark 2:4). Luke's word keramoi means clay roof tiles, common in the Greek and Roman cities his readers knew. Most scholars think Luke described the scene in terms familiar to his audience, as a modern preacher might; a few think some houses in Galilee could have had tiles. Luke is less concerned with building methods than with the friends' determination.

a: your sins have been forgiven you
p: The perfect passive means God has forgiven, and the forgiveness stands. Jesus does not say "I forgive you."
b: Jewish writers often used the passive to avoid naming God. Jesus announces that the man's sins are forgiven. The scribes hear more: a man claiming to speak God's pardon without a priest, a sacrifice or the temple. Many in Jesus' world linked illness and sin (John 9:2), and a later rabbinic saying holds that a sick man does not recover until all his sins are forgiven (Babylonian Talmud, Nedarim 41a). Jesus speaks to the deeper need first. "Man" is a normal form of address in Greek, as in 12:14 and 22:58, not a rude one. On confession and absolution in the churches, see the cards at Matthew 9 and Psalm 32.
orig: ἀφέωνταί σοι αἱ ἁμαρτίαι σου (apheōntai soi hai hamartiai sou)

p: Only God forgives sins. But Israel's prophets could announce God's forgiveness, as Nathan did to David.
b: In Isaiah God is the one "who wipes away your rebellions for my own sake" (Isaiah 43:25). Yet a prophet could declare it: Nathan told David, "The LORD, for his part, has put away your sin" (2 Samuel 12:13), and priests declared atonement made through sacrifice. Scholars such as E. P. Sanders doubt that announcing forgiveness was, strictly, blasphemy under Jewish law, which later defined it as pronouncing the divine name (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5). The scribes' charge in the story reflects the impression that Jesus was acting in God's place, and Luke means the reader to see that he is.

t: The Son of Man, first use in Luke
p: Jesus' favorite way of speaking of himself. It can mean "a human being" and also the heavenly figure of Daniel 7.
b: In Hebrew and Aramaic "son of man" means simply a human being (Psalm 8:4; Ezekiel 2:1). In Daniel 7:13–14 "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds and receives authority and a kingdom from God. In the Gospels the phrase is Jesus' way of speaking of himself; others use it only when echoing him (the crowd in John 12:34), and after Easter only Stephen uses it (Acts 7:56). Here it joins both senses: a human being on earth who holds an authority that Daniel's figure receives in heaven. The words "on earth" matter: forgiveness is not only a future heavenly verdict but is given here and now.
orig: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthrōpou)

p: The word is the source of English "paradox": things contrary to what anyone expected.
b: Paradoxa appears only here in the New Testament. Greek writers used it for marvels and unexpected turns of events. The crowd's reaction comes in three steps, astonishment (ekstasis, being beside oneself), glorifying God, and fear, the usual response to God's acts in Luke (1:65; 7:16). Their "today" echoes Jesus' "Today" in Nazareth (4:21).

a: a man named Levi, a tax collector
p: Mark and Luke call him Levi; Matthew's Gospel calls him Matthew. Luke's list of the Twelve has a Matthew but no Levi.
b: Mark 2:14 names him "Levi son of Alphaeus," and Matthew 9:9 tells the same story of "a man ... His name was Matthew." Luke 6:15 lists Matthew among the Twelve but does not say he is Levi. Most traditional readers think one man had two names (as Simon was also Peter); some suppose "Matthew" was the name given at his call. Many critical scholars think the Gospel of Matthew transferred the story to the apostle Matthew, whom tradition linked with that Gospel. Either way, a tax collector becomes a follower.

p: Levi probably collected tolls on goods passing along the road and the lake, for Herod Antipas.
b: Capernaum lay near the border between Antipas' Galilee and Philip's territory to the east, on a road from Damascus to the coast. Goods crossing the border paid duties, collected at a booth (telōnion). Galilee was ruled by Antipas, not directly by Rome, so Levi worked for the Jewish client king, though the system served Rome. Such collectors were seen as dishonest and as compromised by constant contact with Gentiles and their money.

a: Levi threw a big reception for him
p: Luke's Jesus is always at table: with tax collectors, Pharisees, crowds, friends, and finally the two at Emmaus.
b: Luke tells of more meals than any other Gospel: Levi's banquet, dinners with Pharisees (7:36; 11:37; 14:1), the feeding of the five thousand (9:12–17), Martha's house (10:38–42), Zacchaeus (19:5–7), the Last Supper (22:14–38), Emmaus (24:30) and a meal with the risen Jesus (24:41–43). Critics said he "eats and drinks" with the wrong people (7:34; 15:2). In the ancient world, eating together meant accepting one another, so the meals act out the welcome Jesus preaches and look ahead to the banquet of God's kingdom (13:29; 14:15).

p: At a formal meal, guests lay on couches propped on the left elbow, with their feet away from the low table.
b: The Greek katakeimai, "recline," reflects the Greek and Roman banquet custom adopted by well-off Jews for feasts and, later, for the Passover meal, as a sign of free people at leisure. English versions often say "eating" or "sitting." The posture explains how a woman could stand behind Jesus at his feet (7:38) and how a disciple could lean against him (John 13:23).

p: The verb is the Greek Old Testament's word for Israel's complaints against Moses and God in the wilderness.
b: Gongyzō imitates the sound of muttering. In the Greek of Exodus 16:7–8 and Numbers 14:27 Israel grumbles against God's provision. Luke uses it again when Pharisees and scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners (15:2) and when the crowd grumbles that he lodges with Zacchaeus (19:7). Each time the complaint is about the company Jesus keeps.

p: Not ordinary people who were careless about purity, according to E. P. Sanders, but people known for breaking God's law.
b: Older scholarship, following Joachim Jeremias, often equated "sinners" with the common people (am ha'aretz) despised by Pharisees for laxity about purity, or with despised trades. E. P. Sanders argued that in Jewish usage "sinners" meant the wicked, people who had in effect left the covenant: robbers, extortioners, moneylenders, prostitutes. The offense was not that Jesus ate with ordinary people but that he welcomed notorious wrongdoers before they had made restitution.
