Other scholars think the label could be stretched to anyone a group judged faithless. Luke's own interest is clear: "to call sinners to repentance" (5:32).

p: Mark and Matthew end, "I came to call sinners." Luke adds "to repentance," a key theme for him.
b: Repentance runs through Luke-Acts: John's baptism (3:3, 8), joy in heaven over one sinner who repents (15:7, 10), the commission to preach "repentance for the forgiveness of sins" to all nations (24:47), Peter's call in Acts 2:38. E. P. Sanders argued that the historical Jesus offered sinners a place in the kingdom without first demanding the usual repentance and restitution, and that this is what scandalized people; on that view Luke's addition clarifies or softens. Others reply that repentance is implied in following Jesus, as with Levi and Zacchaeus. The "righteous" may be meant ironically (those who think they are) or plainly (those who are, like Zechariah and Elizabeth, 1:6).

a: often fast and say their prayers
t: Fasting and prayer among the devout
p: Devout Jews fasted beyond the Day of Atonement. Luke's Pharisee boasts of fasting twice a week.
b: The Law commanded one fast a year (Leviticus 16:29–31), but pious Jews added private fasts. The Pharisee in Jesus' parable boasts of fasting twice a week (18:12), and the early Christian Didache tells believers not to fast on Mondays and Thursdays "with the hypocrites" but on Wednesdays and Fridays (Didache 8:1), which shows the Jewish custom of two weekly fasts. Luke alone adds "prayers": John taught his disciples a prayer (11:1). The question is not whether to fast but why Jesus' followers are feasting.

p: Literally "the sons of the wedding hall," a Semitic idiom for the groom's attendants. A wedding was a week of feasting.
b: Jewish weddings could last seven days (Judges 14:12; Tobit 11:18), and the groom's companions were excused from some duties so they could celebrate. The prophets pictured God as Israel's husband: "With a bridegroom's joy over his bride / your God will rejoice over you" (Isaiah 62:5; compare Hosea 2:19–20). By calling himself the groom, Jesus takes a role Scripture gives to God. John the Baptist uses the image of himself as the groom's friend in John 3:29.
orig: τοὺς υἱοὺς τοῦ νυμφῶνος (tous huious tou nymphōnos)
r: Isaiah 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20; John 3:29; Mark 2:19; Matthew 9:15; Revelation 19:7

a: the groom will be taken away from them
t: The first hint of his death
p: "Taken away" points to Jesus' death. The verb recalls the servant of Isaiah 53, taken away from the land of the living.
b: Aparthē, "be taken away," is used only in this saying in the New Testament. Many hear Isaiah 53:8, where the Greek says "his life is taken from the earth" (the Hebrew: "He was cut off from the land of the living," Isaiah 53:8). The saying explains why the church fasts after Easter, a practice the Didache and later church calendars confirm. Whether Christians should keep set fast days is discussed on the card at Matthew 6, which covers both Matthew 6:16 and Matthew 9:15.

a: Nobody tears a patch from a new coat
p: In Mark the patch is unshrunk cloth. In Luke it is cut from a new coat, so the folly is double: two coats ruined.
b: Mark's saying is about a practical problem: new cloth shrinks and tears the old garment (Mark 2:21). Luke makes the picture absurd: someone tears up a new coat to mend an old one, ruining the new and still not fixing the old. Luke uses one verb twice, schizō, "tear": the man tears the patch from the new coat, and so "he will tear the new coat." Readings: (1) Jesus' new way cannot be used to patch up the old system of fasting and piety; (2) both old and new have value, and neither should be destroyed for the other; (3) Luke's change shows his concern that the new not be wasted. The parable comes in reply to the question about fasting, so the "old" is the pattern of piety the critics expect.

p: Wine was stored in goatskins. New wine still fermenting stretched the skin; an old, stiff skin would split.
b: A whole goat hide, sewn up, held wine. Fresh skins were elastic; old ones dried out and cracked (Psalm 119:83; Joshua 9:13). Fermenting wine gives off gas and swells, so it needed a skin that could stretch. The saying says that the new life Jesus brings needs new forms. Christians have applied it to many things: the gospel and the Law, new churches and old institutions, and new believers and old habits.

a: no one who has been drinking the old wants the new
p: Only Luke has this saying. It seems to praise the old, after two sayings about the new. What does it mean?
b: Readings: (1) Irony: people who like the old do not even want to try the new, which explains why Jesus' critics reject him; this is the most common view. (2) A warning to the church: Jewish tradition is good, and those who love it should not be despised; Luke elsewhere honors the Law and the temple. (3) A plain wine-lover's proverb, like Sirach's "New friend, new wine: give it time to age, and you will enjoy drinking it" (Sirach 9:10), meaning people need time to get used to the new. Some ancient witnesses leave the verse out, perhaps because it seemed to contradict 5:36–38; others read "better" for "good" (see the variant).
